content: The use of NRTI backbones in fixed-dose combinations is strongly recommended as the preferred approach for antiretroviral therapy (ART), supported by moderate-quality evidence. Heat-stable fixed-dose combinations of atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) are the preferred boosted protease inhibitor (PI) options for second-line ART, also supported by moderate-quality evidence. A heat-stable fixed-dose combination of darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) can be used as an alternative boosted PI option for second-line ART, though this is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Additionally, a combination of raltegravir (RAL) plus LPV/r may serve as an alternative second-line ART regimen, with a conditional recommendation and low-quality evidence. Viral load testing should be conducted early after initiating ART (within six months), at 12 months, and then at least annually to detect treatment failure. If viral load testing is not routinely available, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure, with targeted viral load testing to confirm viral failure when possible. For service delivery recommendations, an additional criterion is the absence of adverse drug reactions requiring regular monitoring. For children, after failure of a first-line LPV/r-based regimen, those younger than three years should switch to a RAL-based second-line regimen (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Children older than three years should switch to a second-line regimen containing two NRTIs plus efavirenz (EFV) or RAL (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). After failure of a first-line NNRTI-based regimen, children should transition to a boosted PI-based regimen, with LPV/r or ATV/r as the preferred options (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Following failure of a first-line regimen of ABC or TDF + 3TC (or FTC), the preferred NRTI backbone for second-line ART is AZT + 3TC (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). National programs should establish policies for third-line ART, which should include new drugs with minimal cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) and second-generation NNRTIs and PIs (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Patients on a failing second-line regimen with no new antiretroviral options should continue with a tolerated regimen (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for adults, including pregnant women, with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). In settings with high prevalence of malaria or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be initiated regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). It may be discontinued in adults who are clinically stable on ART, with evidence of immune recovery and viral suppression (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). However, in high-prevalence settings, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should continue regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for all HIV-infected patients with active TB disease, regardless of CD4 count (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). For infants, children, and adolescents with HIV, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended irrespective of clinical and immune conditions, with priority given to children under five years old and those with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or CD4 ≤350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). In high-prevalence settings, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should continue until adulthood, regardless of ART provision (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). In low-prevalence settings, it may be discontinued for children aged five years and older who are clinically stable and virally suppressed on ART for at least six months, with a CD4 count >350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is also recommended for HIV-exposed infants from 4–6 weeks of age until HIV infection is excluded by appropriate testing after breastfeeding cessation (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). For tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis in HIV-associated TB or multidrug-resistant TB, Xpert MTB/RIF is recommended over conventional microscopy, culture, and drug susceptibility testing (DST) as the initial diagnostic test for adults and children (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence for adults; very low-quality evidence for children). It is also preferred for cerebrospinal fluid specimens in suspected TB meningitis cases (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Xpert MTB/RIF may replace conventional methods for testing non-respiratory specimens in suspected extrapulmonary TB cases (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) is recommended for adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB, based on clinical screening, regardless of tuberculin skin test (TST) status, degree of immunosuppression, ART status, or pregnancy (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). IPT should also be provided for at least 36 months in individuals with unknown or positive TST status and no active TB (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Children living with HIV who do not have poor weight gain, fever, or current cough are unlikely to have active TB and should receive IPT if TB is ruled out (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Routine antifungal primary prophylaxis is not recommended for CrAg-negative individuals or those with unknown CrAg status prior to ART initiation unless ART initiation is delayed (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). ART initiation should be deferred in patients with cryptococcal meningitis until there is sustained clinical response to antifungal therapy, typically after 4–6 weeks of treatment (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). For cardiovascular risk and depression, assessment and management should be included in HIV care services for all individuals living with HIV (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Community-based interventions, adherence clubs, and peer support are recommended to improve retention in care (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Less frequent clinical visits (every 3–6 months) and medication pickups are recommended for stable patients on ART (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Task-shifting to trained lay providers for ART distribution and initiation by non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses is also recommended (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).
